doc.title: Rufus Reid interviewed by Monk Rowe, Atlanta, GA, January 4, 2013

title: Playing on top of or behind the beat
summary: The width of the beat, Mel Lewis, Jack DeJohnette and Elvin Jones, and bass and drums compromising on pulse.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: Well you just said something that makes me think about, is there such a thing as playing on top of the beat or behind the beat?

Oh absolutely. Absolutely. This is what I also work with the bass players. Because we have the pulse. This is a quarter note: one-two-three-four one-two-three-four. But that’s not the pulse. The pulse is [hand gesture] and a bigger pulse is [hand gesture]. So there’s a lot of things that can be done within the pulse. And the beat is actually this wide, and the center of the beat is here. Some people play over here, some people play it here, some people play it here. That’s what it’s like, and this zone over here. But drummers are more vivid with that. You know when I got a chance to play with Mel Lewis, he plays so, his beat was so wide that if you were a bass player and you couldn’t play with Mel Lewis, something was terribly wrong. But Jack DeJohnette played more up on the beat, much more in front of the middle. But you can’t measure it. I mean there is no ruler that says — but it is a feeling. Elvin Jones was really kind of more like Mel Lewis. They were really — so it was different. And as a bass player I think the rhythm section players, bass players and drummers, have to find — we have to be pliable. We have to be more like silly putty. We have to be able to compromise and find — because everybody has a different — we all have a different gait when we walk — because we’re individuals. There’s something a little bit different. We are all walking, and we’re walking the same tempo, but we have a different gait. And so I think when we play this music, some things you can play and manage — people just float. They dance, and some people are much more stiff when they play. It’s that pulse. And I think bass players and drummers have to — because that’s my first job is to find and compromise with that drummer. And he or she has to do that with me. And then the piano player has no choice.
Here it is, right here. You fit in.

That’s exactly correct. And then when the piano player comes with us, the trio, then the horn players have to come with us. They have no choice. But it becomes this huge carpet for them to just have fun. To me, that’s how I think of — because I can play by myself and do whatever I want. And I can ritard and race and do this — but once you enter the picture and we’re going to play a duet together and we’re going to actually have

conversations, then I have to give you an opportunity to have a conversation. It’s the same thing with the playing, and you come together. To me this is the magic that can not be put in a book. It can’t be on page 12. It just cannot be.
